docs.title: convomem-arena
docs.text:
convomem-arena turns Salesforce ConvoMem (paper, reference code) into tasks for evaluation and reinforcement learning. Each task asks a question about a user's earlier conversations with an assistant: a fact the user stated, something the assistant recommended, a detail that later changed, a preference to respect, or something that was never said at all. The answer is buried in a history that also holds many unrelated conversations from the same person.

The same tasks reach the agent in three ways, so you can measure long-context recall and agentic memory use on identical data:

memory_mode What the agent gets Tests context (default) The full history in the prompt, using ConvoMem's official answer prompt Long-context recall (the paper's baseline) tools Only the question; the history sits behind a per-rollout MCP memory server Agentic retrieval: deciding what to look up, and when files Only the question; the history is written to memory/conversation_NNN.txt Memory as a filesystem, with general-purpose tools

Answers are graded by ConvoMem's official RIGHT/WRONG judges, one per category, and in tools mode the environment also measures whether the agent actually retrieved the evidence.

docs.title: The dataset
docs.text:
Source: Salesforce/ConvoMem on Hugging Face, pinned to revision e3e9b39115b02346824c70d349350de738f8be41. 75,336 question–answer items across 100 synthetic personas (CRM-flavored professions: Account Executive, Data Architect, Telemarketer, …).

The environment reads two folders:

core_benchmark/
├── evidence_questions/<category>_evidence/<N>_evidence/<persona-uuid>_<Title>.json   # questions + evidence conversations
└── filler_conversations/<persona-uuid>_<Title>.json                                  # 400 unrelated conversations per persona

Each evidence item looks like this, abridged from a real record:

{
  "question": "For the new software vendor contract, what was the precise liability cap in USD that I established as my absolute non-negotiable limit?",
  "answer": "You set your absolute non-negotiable liability cap for the new vendor at $2,500,000.",
  "message_evidences": [{"speaker": "User", "text": "...my absolute walk-away is a $2.5M cap..."}],
  "conversations": [{"id": "…", "messages": [{"speaker": "User", "text": "…"}, {"speaker": "Assistant", "text": "…"}]}],
  "personId": "af47b47b-…", "category": "Professional Life", "scenario_description": "…"
}

docs.title: Categories
docs.text:
Category (--env.taskset.categories) Folder What it tests Evidence counts Example user_facts user_evidence Recall of facts the user stated, possibly combined across messages 1–6 "What liability cap did I set?" → "$2,500,000" assistant_facts assistant_facts_evidence Recall of what the assistant itself said or recommended 1–6 "What KPI did you suggest for the advocacy program?" → "Advocate Sourced Revenue" changing_facts changing_evidence Tracking updates; only the latest value is correct 2–6 "When is the CRM update scheduled?" → the last rescheduled date abstention abstention_evidence Recognizing that the answer was never given 1–3 "What is the projected contract value…?" → should say it doesn't know preferences preference_evidence Recommendations that respect stated preferences; the answer is a rubric 1–2 "Recommend a lightweight PM tool" → rubric: simple, visual tools implicit_connections implicit_connection_evidence Connecting indirect context; the answer is a rubric 1–3 "How should we streamline proposals?" → rubric: agile, low-bureaucracy

The evidence count is the number of conversations the evidence is spread across. Multi-evidence items require combining information from several conversations.

To audit items before trusting results on them, see data quality.

Speaker labels in the raw data mix User/user and Assistant/assistant. They're normalized to User / Assistant.

docs.title: context: the long-context baseline
docs.text:
The prompt is ConvoMem's official answer prompt (EvaluationUtils.getModelAnswerPrompt), with the history laid out exactly as buildConversationContext does it:

Answer the question based on the conversations below. If the User in the conversation refers to themselves ("I", "me", "my"), they are the person being asked about. Be direct and factual.

Conversation 1:
User: I'm trying to decide on a hike for this weekend…
Assistant: …

Conversation 2:
…

Question: <question>

Answer:

A conversation averages roughly 6,000 characters (~1.5k tokens). Rough prompt sizes:

context_size ≈ prompt tokens 1 1.5k 10 15k 30 45k 100 150k 300 450k

In this mode TaskData.conversations is left empty, because the history is already in the prompt and storing it twice would double memory.

docs.title: tools: agentic memory over MCP
docs.text:
The prompt contains only the question and the number of stored conversations:

Answer the question based on your past conversations with the User. The 20 conversations, in chronological order, are available through the memory tools. If the User in the conversations refers to themselves ("I", "me", "my"), they are the person being asked about. Be direct and factual.

Question: <question>

A per-rollout MCP server (MemoryToolset, TOOL_PREFIX = "memory") receives the task's history in setup_task and exposes:

Tool Signature Returns memory_search (query: str, limit: int = 8) Top messages by Okapi BM25 (k1=1.5, b=0.75, light stopword list), each with conversation, message, speaker, full text. limit is clamped to 1–20 memory_read_conversation (conversation: int, start: int = 1, count: int = 40) Consecutive messages of one conversation (1-based numbering) plus total_messages. count is clamped to 1–100 memory_list_conversations (offset: int = 0, limit: int = 50) total_conversations and, per conversation, num_messages and the first 200 characters of its opening user message

Every search or read records which conversations it surfaced on the shared MemoryState, which scoring reads back as retrieval metrics. Listing counts as a tool call but not as retrieval.

This is the mode for long histories (100–300 conversations) that don't fit in context, which is the regime the ConvoMem paper studies with memory systems.

docs.title: files: memory as a filesystem
docs.text: Task.setup writes one file per conversation (memory/conversation_001.txt is the oldest) relative to the runtime's working directory. The prompt points the agent there and asks for the answer as the final message. There are no custom tools: the agent uses whatever the harness gives it (bash's grep/cat, Claude Code's file tools, …). That follows prime-envs' preference for general harness tools over custom ones. Run this mode on docker or prime (see Limitations).

docs.title: Reward
docs.text: Name Weight Value correct 1.0 1.0 if the category's ConvoMem judge says RIGHT, else 0.0. An empty final reply scores 0.0 without calling the judge. With fact-scoring exact_match, the three fact categories use the deterministic check below instead

docs.title: Exact match for fact categories
docs.text:
A sanity check, not a benchmark score

Exact match is meant as a cheap sanity check that the environment runs end to end and that replies contain the expected facts, with no judge endpoint and no cost. For any full-scale evaluation, published result or leaderboard, always use the official judges (the default, fact-scoring judge), and keep the judge model fixed across compared runs.

The official judges make scores comparable with the ConvoMem paper, but each one is a model call: it costs time and money, needs an endpoint, and can vary between runs. For user_facts, assistant_facts and changing_facts there is a deterministic alternative.

ConvoMem's gold answers are full sentences, so a literal comparison almost never matches. Instead a reply matches when it contains the answer's details: the names and numbers the question doesn't already contain. "The concert has been postponed to April 10th of next year" needs april and 10. Answers with no names or numbers fall back to their content words. The answer and the reply are read the same way: accents are dropped (Brené = Brene), dotted abbreviations closed (a.m. = AM), letters split from digits (XY123456 = XY 123456), and numbers are compared only with numbers ($2,100 is 2100, not 2 and 100).

Four guards keep it from being gamed when used as a training reward:

  • No dumping: a reply longer than max(100, 5 × the answer's words) scores 0.
  • No candidate lists: a reply scores 0 when it offers more than 8 names or numbers that neither the answer nor the question contains, 3 or more making up over half its words, 2 or more in a reply that is at least 75% names and numbers, or 3 or more new words with almost no function words (a list in lower case). "Liam Petrov, Acme, Boston" fails; "Liam Petrov, from Acme Corp in Boston." passes.
  • No hedging or denial: a reply scores 0 when it voices doubt the answer doesn't (I don't remember, maybe, not sure, wrong), when the sentences stating the answer's details use not, no, never, or, either, neither or n't more often than the answer does, or when a sentence of its own rejects or adds an alternative (Nope., That's not right., Or October.).
  • No stale numbers (changing_facts): a reply that also states a number from an earlier evidence message, one the latest message and the answer no longer contain, scores 0. "October 5th or April 10th" fails; "postponed from the original October date to April 10th" passes.

It is recorded as the exact_match metric on every fact-category rollout, whatever the reward uses, so the two can be compared on any run. To make it the reward and skip the judge for those categories:

vf-run convomem-arena ... --env.taskset.task.fact-scoring exact_match

The other three categories always use their judge: abstention and the two rubric categories have no string to match.

How well it agrees with the judge. On 36 replies the judge had graded (24 from local runs and 12 from a Vellum memory evaluation), exact match gave the same verdict every time. Those were ordinary replies, so they say nothing about replies written to game the check.

How hard it is to game. Issue #11 showed that the first version gave full credit to denied or hedged answers ("It is not April 10th."), to a list of the history's names on 30–39% of tasks, and failed about 1.5% of gold answers on themselves. On the 8,451 fact items of the cached evidence files (pinned revision), the current version:

Reply Scores 1.0 (before → now) the gold answer itself, or lower-cased, or with a friendly opener or closer 98.5% → 99.9–100% the gold answer plus a few more names 98.5% → 99.5% the gold answer plus the latest evidence message quoted 98.5% → 94.2% I don't remember. It is not this: + gold 98.5% → 0.1% gold + No, that is wrong, and I don't remember… 98.5% → 0.0% Either (another answer) or gold. I can't tell which. 95.2% → 2.9% gold + That is not it. 98.5% → 1.0% Not + gold 98.5% → 15.0% (another answer); gold 96.2% → 89.2% every name and number of the evidence conversation, up to 100 words 49.6% → 16.0% (23.2% in lower case)

What it still can't do: tell an alternative from extra detail when nothing marks it (a bare "W; R"), catch a denial worded in a way the phrase lists don't cover, or stop a short list padded with function words. A word-level check cannot reliably separate a denial from ordinary text, which is why exact match is a sanity check: use the official judges for full-scale evaluation, for leaderboards, and whenever a reward will be optimized against. The judge-robustness miss also still holds: in "a Caprese salad, a tomato basil pasta sauce and pesto" only "Caprese" is a name, so a reply that gets the other two dishes wrong still passes.

docs.title: Judges
docs.text:
The judge prompts are copied verbatim from the reference implementation (questions/evidence/generation/AnsweringEvaluation.scala). Each category uses the same evaluator the paper does:

Category Reference evaluator Class Judge sees user_facts (1 evidence) UserFactsAnsweringEvaluation (single) UserFactsSingleJudge question, evidence message, gold answer, response user_facts (2+ evidence) UserFactsAnsweringEvaluation (multi) UserFactsMultiJudge question, numbered evidence messages, gold answer, response assistant_facts, changing_facts DefaultAnsweringEvaluation ConvoMemJudge question, gold answer, response abstention AbstentionAnsweringEvaluation AbstentionJudge question, response (a refusal or "I don't know" is RIGHT) preferences, implicit_connections RubricBasedAnsweringEvaluation RubricAnswerJudge question, rubric, response (must satisfy all criteria)

Verdict parsing follows the reference: a reply containing only RIGHT → pass; WRONG, or both RIGHT and WRONG → fail; neither → raise. Raising rather than returning 0.0 means a broken judge shows up as an error instead of being recorded as a model mistake.

The judge endpoint defaults to verifiers' JudgeConfig (Prime Inference, key from PRIME_API_KEY). The paper used GPT-4o-mini and Gemini Flash during data validation. Pick a judge and keep it fixed when comparing runs, and check how far you can trust it with the judge robustness checker.

docs.title: Metrics (recorded in tools mode only)
docs.text:
Name Meaning memory_tool_calls Number of memory tool calls in the rollout evidence_recall Fraction of evidence conversations returned by at least one memory_search or memory_read_conversation call conversations_retrieved Distinct conversations the agent retrieved

These are metrics, not rewards, so they're logged for analysis and never trained on. Rewarding recall directly would encourage the agent to dump the whole history. To experiment with it as a shaping signal, see plugged rewards.

docs.title: How a task is built
docs.text:
For every evidence item and every requested context size, the taskset builds one task. Mixing follows ConvoMem's official StandardTestCasesGenerator:

  1. Keep all evidence. Every evidence conversation of the item is included, even when context_size is smaller than the evidence count. The context size is a target for dilution, not a hard cap.
  2. Sample filler from the same persona. Draw context_size − evidence_count conversations from that persona's 400 filler conversations, so the distractors are on-topic for the same person.
  3. Place the evidence at random sorted positions. Evidence conversations go at random positions in their original order, which matters for changing_facts, where the order defines which value is current.
  4. Seed everything. The RNG is random.Random(f"{seed}:{task_id}"), so a given seed and task ID always produce the same history.

The task ID encodes the full provenance and doubles as the task key:

user_evidence/1_evidence/af47b47b-…_Procurement_Manager/17/ctx30
└─ folder ──┘└─ count ─┘└──────── persona file ────────┘└item┘└size┘

docs.title: Ordering and laziness
docs.text:
load() is a generator, and dataset files download from the Hub only when first needed (they're cached in the standard HF cache). Tasks are interleaved:

  • round-robin across categories (in categories order), and within each category
  • round-robin across evidence counts, then
  • persona files and items in a seeded shuffled order, then
  • one task per context size for each item.

So -n 6 --env.taskset.context-sizes 10 gives one task from each category and downloads only a few MB. -n 12 with two context sizes gives the same six items at both sizes. That makes context-size comparisons paired.

docs.title: verifiers, prime-envs and the Hub
docs.text:
Piece Role In this project verifiers (import verifiers.v1 as vf) Framework: tasks, tools, judges, rewards, and the runner that puts an agent on a task and records a trace Every class here subclasses a vf.* base prime-envs Prime Intellect's repo of first-party environments; the source of conventions (layout, prompting rules, README style) This package follows those conventions and can drop in as environments/<group>/convomem_arena Environments Hub Registry where environment packages are published and installed by ID (owner/name@version) Packaged as convomem-arena, the ID it would be installed by

verifiers v0 vs. v1. Older tutorials and many Hub environments (listed as Legacy) use the v0 API: load_environment(), vf.SingleTurnEnv, vf.ToolEnv, vf-eval. The current release (verifiers>=0.4.1) ships only v1: Taskset / Task / TaskData, @vf.reward, vf.Toolset, and the vf-validate / vf-run CLIs. This package is v1 only.

docs.title: verifiers v1 concepts, mapped to this code
docs.text:
verifiers concept What it is Here vf.TaskData One immutable row: the prompt plus hidden fields for scoring ConvoMemData in models.py vf.Task Behavior for one row: setup, stop conditions, toolsets, rewards, metrics ConvoMemTask in taskset.py vf.Taskset Loader that yields tasks from load() ConvoMemTaskset in taskset.py vf.TasksetConfig Load-time knobs → --env.taskset.* flags ConvoMemConfig vf.TaskConfig Per-task runtime and scoring knobs → --env.taskset.task.* flags ConvoMemTaskConfig vf.State Mutable per-rollout state shared between tool servers and scoring MemoryState in models.py vf.Toolset + @vf.tool Custom tools served over MCP MemoryToolset in servers/memory.py vf.Judge LLM grader: a prompt template plus a parse function ConvoMemJudge and its subclasses in judges.py @vf.reward(weight=…) Score that adds score × weight to trace.reward correct @vf.metric Logged measurement that never affects the reward memory (tool calls, evidence recall) @vf.stop Predicate that ends the rollout early turn_limit Harness Agent program that talks to the model (null, bash, claude_code, …), chosen at run time Not fixed by this taskset Runtime Where the harness runs (subprocess, docker, prime), chosen at run time Not fixed by this taskset Trace The full record of a rollout, saved to traces.jsonl See Reading results

The taskset ID maps to the module: convomem-arena → import convomem_arena → the class listed in __all__ (ConvoMemTaskset). That's the only thing convomem_arena/__init__.py does.

docs.title: Rollout lifecycle
docs.text:
ConvoMemTaskset.load() ──yields──▶ ConvoMemTask(ConvoMemData, ConvoMemTaskConfig)
                                          │
  1. Task.setup(trace, runtime)           │  records trace.info["convomem"];
                                          │  files mode: writes memory/conversation_NNN.txt
  2. Task.toolsets(config)                │  tools mode: launches one MemoryToolset per rollout,
                                          │  which loads the history in setup_task(task_data)
  3. Harness runs the model ◀────────────┘  prompt = TaskData.prompt; MCP tools if any;
       │                                     @vf.stop turn_limit checked before each model call
  4. Scoring
       ├─ @vf.metric memory    → memory_tool_calls, evidence_recall, conversations_retrieved
       └─ @vf.reward correct   → ConvoMem judge for the category → RIGHT = 1.0, WRONG = 0.0
                                          │
  5. Trace written to traces.jsonl ◀──────┘

docs.title: Quick start: evaluate a personal assistant
docs.text:
The model quick start hands the history to the model. A personal assistant is never handed its history: it hears each conversation once, decides what to remember, files it away, and has to find it again later. To test that, the assistant has to live through the conversations first.

convomem_arena.vellum_eval does this for Vellum, an open-source personal assistant with its own memory system. The same four stages apply to any assistant with a memory you can fill and query.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Plan. Pick N questions per category for one persona, and merge their evidence conversations (plus filler from the same persona) into one time-ordered history, one day apart and ending yesterday. One memory then answers every question.
  2. Build. Import the history into a clean Vellum instance, let Vellum's own memory retrospective review each conversation and call remember, force a consolidation pass that files the facts into concept pages, and save the result as a vellum backup snapshot. This is the slow part, so it is cached.
  3. Ask. With memory writing switched off, ask each question in a new conversation. The reply is read from the turn's MLflow trace, and the injected memory from Vellum's memory-v3 pool log.
  4. Score. Grade with ConvoMem's official judge prompts (any OpenAI-compatible endpoint; default local Ollama), plus two rough diagnostics for fact categories: is the answer anywhere in memory (capture), and was it in what got injected (retrieval).

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
python -m convomem_arena.vellum_eval.run \
  --source /path/to/vellum-assistant \
  --instance vellum-rsi-eval --persona Small_Business_Owner \
  --per-category 2 --history-size 16

--source is a vellum-assistant checkout (with cli/ and assistant/), and --instance a hatched instance. To run the stages separately, use --stages build, then --stages ask,score --run-dir outputs/vellum-eval/<run-id>. Each run writes plan.json, build.json, answers.jsonl, scores.jsonl and a report.md with accuracy per category.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
Use a dedicated instance

The build restores snapshots over the instance's workspace. Never point it at an assistant you use day to day.

  • A freshly hatched instance with mlflowTracing.enabled, connections and profiles for every call site, and a Claude Code token stored if call sites use the claude-code provider. A snapshot restore wipes that token's value, so set it again after each restore.
  • A clean shell environment. The harness strips VELLUM_WORKSPACE_DIR and *_IPC_SOCKET_DIR inherited from your shell; a profile that exports another instance's values would otherwise make daemons bind that instance's socket.
  • One persona per instance for now. vellum backup bundles exclude the Qdrant vector index, and a restore keeps the live one, so restoring persona B over persona A leaves A's vectors behind. Restoring a persona's own snapshot is fine.
  • Time. Retrospectives take about 3–5 minutes per conversation on a local 30B model, so a 17-conversation history takes about an hour to build.

docs.title: Reading the result
docs.text:
A low score has four possible causes, and the diagnostics help separate them: the fact was never captured, consolidation dropped it, retrieval didn't inject it, or the model had it and still answered wrong. Below ten concept pages, Vellum's memory v3 runs a lean profile that skips its selector, so a small history never tests retrieval; the report says so when that happens.

Only want to test Vellum's model?

To run the ordinary benchmark with a Vellum assistant answering from a history in its prompt, see Use a Vellum assistant as the model.

docs.title: Quick start: evaluate a model
docs.text: You need Python ≥ 3.11 and uv.

docs.title: 1. Install
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/rahmansunny071/convomem-arena.git
cd convomem-arena
uv venv --python 3.12
uv pip install -e ".[dev]"

docs.title: 2. Check that tasks load
docs.text:
This builds six tasks, one per category, and sets each one up. It makes no model calls and needs no API key.

uv run vf-validate convomem-arena -n 6 --only-setup --runtime.type subprocess

-n 6 already covers all six categories, because tasks are interleaved across categories (why).

docs.title: 3. Run your first episodes
docs.text:
The run needs two models: the agent that answers, and the judge that grades the answer.

Prime InferenceLocal (Ollama)

By default both use Prime Inference, with the key in PRIME_API_KEY.

export PRIME_API_KEY=...
uv run vf-run convomem-arena -n 6 -r 1 -m <model> \
  --env.agent.harness.id null --env.agent.runtime.type subprocess

docs.title: Run fully local with Ollama
docs.text:
No API key needed: qwen3:30b-a3b serves as both the agent and the judge (verified end to end: 6/6, mean reward 1.000).

# Ollama must be serving the model at 127.0.0.1:11434 first:
#   ollama pull qwen3:30b-a3b && ollama run qwen3:30b-a3b "reply with one word: ok"

export OLLAMA_FAKE_KEY=unused   # ignored by Ollama; vf-run just needs the variable set

uv run vf-run convomem-arena -n 6 -r 1 -m qwen3:30b-a3b \
  --client.base-url http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1 --client.api-key-var OLLAMA_FAKE_KEY \
  --env.agent.harness.id null --env.agent.runtime.type subprocess \
  --env.taskset.context-sizes 10 \
  --env.taskset.task.judge.base-url http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1 \
  --env.taskset.task.judge.api-key-var OLLAMA_FAKE_KEY \
  --env.taskset.task.judge.model qwen3:30b-a3b

A smoke test, not a measurement

A 30B model judging its own transcript is weaker than a frontier judge on the rubric-graded categories (preferences, implicit_connections). Ten conversations of history is also an easy setting. Treat a perfect score here as "it works", not as a result.

docs.title: 4. Look at the results
docs.text: vf-run writes one line per episode to traces.jsonl. Reading results shows which fields matter and how to compute accuracy per category.

docs.title: Reading results
docs.text:
vf-run writes <output_dir>/<run-name>/traces.jsonl with one episode per line. Useful fields:

Path Content task.data.id Provenance ID (folder / count / persona / item / ctx) task.data.category, .evidence_count, .context_size, .num_conversations Slicing keys task.data.question, .answer, .evidence_positions Ground truth traces[0].rewards.correct.score 1.0 / 0.0 traces[0].metrics memory_tool_calls, evidence_recall, conversations_retrieved (tools mode) traces[0].info.convomem Category, evidence count, context size, mode traces[0].info.judge_calls Exact judge request and response traces[0].stop_condition e.g. agent_completed, turn_limit

Per-category accuracy:

import json, collections, sys

acc = collections.defaultdict(list)
for line in open(sys.argv[1]):
    ep = json.loads(line)
    d, t = ep["task"]["data"], ep["traces"][0]
    acc[(d["category"], d["context_size"])].append(t["rewards"]["correct"]["score"])

for (cat, size), xs in sorted(acc.items()):
    print(f"{cat:<22} ctx={size:<4} acc={sum(xs)/len(xs):.3f} n={len(xs)}")

docs.title: Running evaluations
docs.text:
# Long-context baseline at two history lengths (paired: same items at both sizes)
uv run vf-run convomem-arena -n 60 -r 1 -m <model> \
  --env.agent.harness.id null --env.agent.runtime.type subprocess \
  --env.taskset.context-sizes 10 30

# Agentic memory on histories too long for context
uv run vf-run convomem-arena -n 60 -r 1 -m <model> \
  --env.agent.harness.id null --env.agent.runtime.type subprocess \
  --env.taskset.task.memory-mode tools --env.taskset.context-sizes 100 300

# Memory as files, solved by a coding harness in an isolated container
uv run vf-run convomem-arena -n 60 -r 1 -m <model> \
  --env.taskset.task.memory-mode files --env.agent.harness.id bash --env.agent.runtime.type docker

# One category only, harder multi-evidence items
uv run vf-run convomem-arena -n 20 -m <model> --env.agent.harness.id null --env.agent.runtime.type subprocess \
  --env.taskset.categories changing_facts --env.taskset.evidence-counts 4 5 6

# Custom judge endpoint (any OpenAI-compatible API)
uv run vf-run convomem-arena -n 6 -m <model> ... \
  --env.taskset.task.judge.base-url https://api.openai.com/v1 \
  --env.taskset.task.judge.api-key-var OPENAI_API_KEY \
  --env.taskset.task.judge.model gpt-4.1-mini

For large-scale evaluation and RL, use prime-rl (uv run eval convomem-arena … from a prime-rl checkout with this package installed).

docs.title: Suggested experiments
docs.text:
• Context-length curve: context mode at sizes 1 10 30 50 100, accuracy per category. The paper reports that long context degrades as histories grow.
  • Context vs. tools: same items and sizes, memory-mode context vs. tools. Where does retrieval overtake the full history?
  • Retrieval vs. reasoning failures: in tools mode, compare correct with evidence_recall. Low recall with a wrong answer is a search failure. High recall with a wrong answer is a reasoning or synthesis failure, which is common on changing_facts.
  • Abstention calibration: does more history (more distractors) make the agent hallucinate more on abstention?

docs.title: Use a Vellum assistant as the model
docs.text:
The local Ollama quick start works because Ollama serves a real OpenAI-compatible /v1/chat/completions endpoint. A locally hatched Vellum assistant does not expose anything like that.

This tests Vellum's model, not its memory

The history is still pasted into the prompt here. To evaluate how Vellum remembers, see Evaluate a personal assistant.

Its closest equivalent is a synchronous, single-shot CLI/IPC call (assistant llm send, aka assistant inference send) with its own {message, systemPrompt?, model?, ...} shape, not OpenAI's {model, messages}. vf-run --client.base-url can't point at it directly.

scripts/vellum_adapter.py bridges the gap: a small, dependency-free (stdlib-only) local HTTP server that speaks OpenAI's /v1/chat/completions on the outside and shells out to assistant llm send --json on the inside, translating the response back into an OpenAI-shaped JSON body.

Scope — read before using: - Only convomem-arena's context memory mode is supported. assistant llm send has no tools parameter, so it cannot do real tool calls — don't point tools mode at it. - Each request blocks on one subprocess hitting one local daemon; there's no real parallelism behind this adapter. Run vf-run with a low --max-concurrent against it (e.g. -c 1 or -c 2), not the default 128. - assistant llm send does not necessarily use your instance's everyday chat activeProfile — it can fall back to a different, advisor-oriented profile that needs a connection you may not have configured (seen locally: it defaulted to an Anthropic profile and failed with provider_connection "..." not found, even though the instance's real chat profile was a working, keyless Ollama one). If you hit that, check assistant config get llm for a profile that IS configured and set VELLUM_PROFILE to its name — see below. - Verified working end to end — 6/6, mean reward 1.000 — using a local Ollama-backed Vellum profile (qwen3:30b-a3b) as both the agent (through this adapter) and the judge.

# 1. Have a hatched Vellum instance with a working model profile. A keyless local one is
#    easiest to get working for this, e.g.:
#      assistant config set services.inference.provider ollama   # only if you don't
#      assistant config set services.inference.model qwen3:30b-a3b   # already have one
#    then confirm which profile name is actually configured and keyless:
#      assistant config get llm   # look for a profile with "provider": "ollama"

# 2. Point the adapter at that instance and your vellum-assistant checkout:
export ASSISTANT_IPC_SOCKET_DIR=...     # same vars your shell already uses to talk
export VELLUM_WORKSPACE_DIR=...         # to the hatched instance (e.g. via a `vellum-env` helper)
export VELLUM_ASSISTANT_DIR=/path/to/vellum-assistant/assistant   # dir containing src/index.ts
export VELLUM_PROFILE=qwen-local        # the keyless profile name from step 1

# 3. Start the adapter (separate terminal, left running):
python3 scripts/vellum_adapter.py       # listens on http://127.0.0.1:8800/v1

# 4. Run convomem-arena against it. The adapter only stands in for the *agent* model —
#    you still need a judge endpoint (PRIME_API_KEY, or a local judge as in the Ollama
#    example in the quick start).
export VELLUM_FAKE_KEY=unused   # value is ignored; vf-run just needs the var set
export PRIME_API_KEY=...

uv run vf-run convomem-arena -n 6 -r 1 -m vellum -c 1 \
  --client.base-url http://127.0.0.1:8800/v1 --client.api-key-var VELLUM_FAKE_KEY \
  --env.agent.harness.id null --env.agent.runtime.type subprocess \
  --env.taskset.context-sizes 10

docs.title: Data quality
docs.text:
python -m convomem_arena.data_check --out outputs/data-check/run1 audits a sample of items with deterministic checks (no model calls). It samples a few items from each of several persona files in every category and evidence-count folder, so the sample is spread across personas.

Check Severity Flags an item when empty_field error the question or answer is empty evidence_count_mismatch error the number of evidence messages differs from the folder's count flagged_conversation_count error conversations marked containsEvidence differ from that count evidence_not_in_conversations error an evidence message has no close match (similarity < 0.85) in any of its conversations evidence_speaker_mismatch error an evidence message's speaker differs from the conversation's evidence_reworded_in_conversation review an evidence message appears only reworded (usually a changed lead-in; the fact is intact) wrong_evidence_speaker review user facts are said by the assistant, or assistant facts by the user answer_restates_question review the answer adds no content words beyond the question answer_name_not_in_evidence review a name in the answer is in neither the evidence nor the question answer_number_not_in_evidence review a number in the answer is not in the evidence (usually a computed total or average) latest_evidence_not_answer review changing facts: an earlier evidence message matches the answer better than the last answer_terms_in_filler review one filler message of the same persona holds the answer's details, including a name question_topic_in_filler review abstention: one filler message holds most of the question's key words duplicate_question review the same question appears in more than one sampled item

An answer's "details" are its names (capitalised words that don't start a sentence) and numbers, list markers excluded: ConvoMem's gold answers are often written-out advice, so their other words rarely appear in the evidence, but their names and numbers should. Filler matches must co-occur in a single message and include a name, since numbers and scattered words recur by coincidence.

First results (2026-11-17, 368 items from 62 personas, filler checked for 25): 290 items had no flags. Structural errors were rare (3 items: one implicit-connections item with two evidence messages in a one-evidence folder, one abstention item whose evidence matches its conversation at only 0.82). 11 items carried evidence only in reworded form, fact intact. Reading every review flag by hand: missing numbers were almost all computed totals and averages (user facts that test arithmetic over memory); one gold answer relied on world knowledge (a recommended city and museum) rather than the user's history; and filler held true conflicts in a few changing-facts items (the gold answer names Jessica as the new Head of Sales Ops while the same persona's filler names Helen Vance), which a random mix can place after the evidence. Other filler hits were harmless repeats of the same fact, or coincidences.

error flags are facts about the file. review flags are heuristic pointers, written with the item's text to review.md for a human to confirm or dismiss. Filler checks download each persona's filler file (about 5.6 MB); --filler-personas caps how many (default 25). Raise --files-per-folder and --items-per-file to audit more, up to the whole dataset.

docs.title: Judge robustness
docs.text:
Every score here is only as good as its judge, so convomem_arena.judge_check tests a judge model with the same rendered prompts and parser the environment uses. It changes one input at a time and checks whether the verdict behaves:

Variant Changes A robust judge question_paraphrase question reworded, same meaning keeps its verdict evidence_paraphrase evidence reworded, same facts keeps its verdict question_negated question reversed or negated flips RIGHT → WRONG (abstention: keeps RIGHT, a refusal still refuses) evidence_changed evidence now contradicts the answer flips RIGHT → WRONG reference_changed gold answer replaced with a different one flips RIGHT → WRONG response_wrong response replaced with a plausible wrong one flips RIGHT → WRONG

The baseline response is the gold answer itself (for the two rubric categories, a generated reply that satisfies the rubric), so the baseline should be RIGHT. A variant is only run against a judge that can see the input it changes: only the user-facts prompts show evidence, and the abstention prompt shows no gold answer. Each check is repeated, and the majority verdict is used; repeats that disagree are reported as the judge's noise floor.

# 1. sample items and generate perturbations with a generator model (cached; review review.md)
python -m convomem_arena.judge_check perturb --per-category 4 --generator-think \
  --out outputs/judge-check/run1

# 2. grade baseline and variants with each judge, 3 repeats each (resumable)
python -m convomem_arena.judge_check judge --run-dir outputs/judge-check/run1 \
  --judge-model qwen3:30b-a3b --judge-model gpt-oss:20b --repeats 3

# 3. score and write report.md
python -m convomem_arena.judge_check report --run-dir outputs/judge-check/run1

First results (2026-11-17, 24 items, 4 per category, 3 repeats, temperature 0):

Judge Correct response judged RIGHT Paraphrase invariance Wrong response / changed reference → WRONG Negated question → WRONG Contradicted evidence → WRONG Unstable groups qwen3:30b-a3b 23/24 30/30 42/42 0/19 0/4 4/122 gpt-oss:20b 22/24 29/30 40/40 0/18 0/4 0/122

Both judges catch a wrong response or a changed reference every time and ignore rewording, but neither notices when the question no longer asks what the response answers, or when the evidence contradicts it: they grade response against reference, not response against question or evidence. So a ConvoMem score from these judges says "the reply states the gold fact", nothing more. The misses on correct responses are all rubric categories, where the prompt demands every criterion. qwen's 4 unstable groups (3 on negated questions) show it is noisiest exactly where it is uncertain. Small samples (only 4 items exercise evidence) make these indications, not measurements.

Endpoints default to local Ollama; any OpenAI-compatible endpoint works with --judge-base-url and --judge-api-key-var. Perturbations are machine-generated and checked only mechanically (present, actually different, numbers kept in paraphrases), so read review.md before trusting a report: a bad paraphrase makes a robust judge look fragile.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
convomem-arena/
├── pyproject.toml              # package "convomem-arena"; deps: verifiers, huggingface-hub
├── README.md                   # intro, quick starts, license
├── mkdocs.yml                  # this documentation site
├── docs/                       # documentation pages
├── uv.lock
├── convomem_arena/
│   ├── __init__.py             # exports ConvoMemTaskset (how verifiers discovers the taskset)
│   ├── taskset.py              # configs, ConvoMemTask (setup/stop/reward/metric), ConvoMemTaskset (load/build), prompts
│   ├── data.py                 # HubSource (lazy HF download), EvidenceStream (seeded round-robin), mix(), formatting
│   ├── models.py               # ConvoMemData (TaskData) and MemoryState (State), shared by taskset and tool server
│   ├── judges.py               # official ConvoMem judge prompts, RIGHT/WRONG parser, category → judge mapping
│   ├── judge_client.py         # call those judges outside a rollout (any OpenAI-compatible endpoint)
│   ├── judge_check/            # judge robustness checker: variants, perturbation generator, runner, report
│   ├── data_check/             # data quality checker: deterministic checks on sampled raw items
│   ├── text.py                 # shared word / key-term helpers for the checkers
│   └── servers/
│       └── memory.py           # MemoryToolset (MCP): BM25 index, search/read/list tools; runnable as a module
└── tests/
    ├── test_convomem.py        # offline tests (no network, no model)
    ├── test_judge_check.py     # judge checker tests with a fake generator and fake judges
    └── test_data_check.py      # data checker tests on hand-built items

docs.title: Data flow
docs.text:
HubSource ── list_repo_tree / hf_hub_download (cached) ──▶ raw JSON
    │
EvidenceStream.category_items()   seeded file order → items, round-robin over evidence counts
    │
round_robin(categories)           interleave categories
    │
ConvoMemTaskset.build(item, filler, size)
    ├─ mix()                      evidence + same-persona filler, seeded positions
    ├─ prompt by memory_mode      context: full transcript | tools/files: question only
    └─ ConvoMemData(...)          hidden: answer, evidence_messages, evidence_positions, conversations

docs.title: Why models.py is separate
docs.text: The memory server runs as its own process (python -m convomem_arena.servers.memory). It receives the rollout's TaskData by importing its class, and it shares MemoryState with the task. Keeping both models in a module that imports neither the taskset nor the server avoids circular imports.

docs.title: Plugging extra rewards
docs.text:
verifiers lets you add or replace hooks from config without touching code. For example, to try evidence recall as a small shaping reward, write a function:

# my_hooks.py
def recall_bonus(task, trace) -> float:
    found = set(task.evidence_positions) & set(trace.state.retrieved)
    return len(found) / max(len(task.evidence_positions), 1)

[env.taskset.task.rewards]
recall_bonus = { fn = "my_hooks.py:recall_bonus", weight = 0.1 }

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text:
• 2026-11-23 (0.1.4): Exact match is documented as a cheap sanity check; use the official judges for full-scale evaluation and leaderboards. Exact match hardened after issue #11: denied, hedged and retracted answers, and lists of candidate names, now score 0; answers and replies are read the same way (accents, a.m., letters glued to digits, hyphenated and possessive names, numbers with separators), so every gold answer matches itself.
  • 2026-11-18: Optional deterministic scoring for the fact categories (fact-scoring exact_match), and an exact_match metric recorded on every fact-category rollout.
  • 2026-11-17: Data quality checker (python -m convomem_arena.data_check): structural checks, answer grounding, changing-fact order, filler contamination and duplicates on a persona-spread sample.

  • 2026-11-16: Judge robustness checker (python -m convomem_arena.judge_check): one-input-at-a-time paraphrase and meaning-change variants, repeated verdicts, per-judge report. The standalone judge client moved to convomem_arena.judge_client.

  • 2026-11-09: Initial release. verifiers v1 taskset with context / tools / files memory modes, official ConvoMem mixing and judges, and retrieval metrics.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: All fields are CLI flags (snake_case → kebab-case) and can also be set in TOML under [env.taskset], using the snake_case field names.

docs.title: Taskset (--env.taskset.*): what gets loaded
docs.text: Flag Type Default Description categories list all six Subset of user_facts assistant_facts changing_facts abstention preferences implicit_connections evidence-counts list[int] | None all Keep only items with these evidence counts context-sizes list[int] [1, 10, 30] Conversations per history; one task per size per item. The paper uses 1 2 3 4 5 6 10 20 30 50 70 100 150 200 300 seed int 0 Seeds item order and every mix repo-id str Salesforce/ConvoMem Dataset repo revision str e3e9b39… Dataset revision (pinned for reproducibility)

docs.title: Task (--env.taskset.task.*): how each task runs and is scored
docs.text: Flag Type Default Description memory-mode context | tools | files context How the history reaches the agent max-turns int ≥ 1 40 Model calls per rollout before turn_limit stops it fact-scoring judge | exact_match judge How the three fact categories are rewarded: the official judge, or the deterministic exact match with no judge call, a cheap sanity check only; use judge for full-scale evaluation and leaderboards judge.model str verifiers default Judge model judge.base-url str Prime Inference OpenAI-compatible judge endpoint judge.api-key-var str PRIME_API_KEY Name of the env var that holds the judge key tools.runtime.type str subprocess Where the memory MCP server runs (tools mode)

docs.title: Common run flags (from verifiers)
docs.text:
Flag Meaning -n / -r Number of tasks / rollouts per task -m Agent model --client.base-url, --client.api-key-var Agent model endpoint --env.agent.harness.id null, bash, claude_code, codex, … --env.agent.runtime.type subprocess, docker, prime (default) --select.include.idx 0:100, -s (shuffle), --select.limit Task selection -o Output directory

Example TOML (convomem.toml, used as uv run vf-run convomem-arena @ convomem.toml -m <model>):

[env.taskset]
categories = ["user_facts", "changing_facts", "abstention"]
context_sizes = [10, 50]
seed = 0

[env.taskset.task]
memory_mode = "tools"
max_turns = 30

[env.agent.harness]
id = "null"

[env.agent.runtime]
type = "subprocess"

vf-validate nests the same settings under [taskset] / [taskset.task] (its flags are --taskset.*) and takes the runtime as --runtime.type.

docs.title: Design decisions
docs.text: Decision Reason verifiers v1, not v0 The current release ships only v1; v0 environments are listed as Legacy on the Hub Mix on the fly instead of using the 25.7 GB pre_mixed_testcases Same official algorithm, any context size, and a few MB per small run instead of ~40 MB files Same-persona filler, evidence order preserved Matches the reference generator; ordering defines the answer for changing_facts Official answer and judge prompts, verbatim Comparable with the paper; the instructions match the reward Judge failures raise Infrastructure errors must not be scored as wrong answers Per-task toolset (not shared) Each rollout has a different history; per-rollout servers isolate state History out of the prompt in tools/files mode The agent must actually use memory; the history lives in hidden TaskData fields Recall as a metric, not a reward Observing retrieval without incentivizing history dumps Generic tool descriptions prime-envs guidance: describe what a tool does, not how to use it for this task files mode prime-envs prefers general harness tools over custom ones; this lets any coding agent use its own Lazy generator plus round-robin -n stays cheap and still covers every category No role prompt ("You are a memory assistant…") prime-envs guidance for RL environments

docs.title: Development and testing
docs.text:
uv pip install -e ".[dev]" ruff

uv run pytest tests                                  # offline tests, no network or model
uv run ruff check convomem_arena tests
uv run ruff format --check convomem_arena tests

# setup check against real Hub data, all three modes
for m in context tools files; do
  uv run vf-validate convomem-arena -n 6 --only-setup --runtime.type subprocess \
    --taskset.task.memory-mode $m --taskset.context-sizes 10
done

tests/test_convomem.py covers: speaker normalization; mixing (evidence kept, order preserved, determinism, contexts smaller than the evidence count); the reference transcript layout; RIGHT/WRONG parsing; the category → judge mapping; evidence substitution in judge prompts; BM25 search, paging and bounds; round-robin ordering; prompt construction per mode; and seed reproducibility. Hub access is replaced by an in-memory FakeSource. tests/test_judge_check.py and tests/test_data_check.py cover the quality checkers with a fake generator, fake judges and hand-built items.

Testing the whole pipeline without an API key: the agent client and the judge both take a base_url. Pointing both at a small scripted OpenAI-compatible server (one that calls memory_search, answers from the result, and returns "RIGHT" to judge prompts) exercises tool-server launch, state sync, metrics and judge dispatch:

uv run vf-run convomem-arena -n 6 -r 1 -m fake \
  --client.base-url http://127.0.0.1:8765/v1 --client.api-key-var FAKE_KEY \
  --env.taskset.task.judge.base-url http://127.0.0.1:8765/v1 --env.taskset.task.judge.api-key-var FAKE_KEY \
  --env.agent.harness.id null --env.agent.runtime.type subprocess --env.taskset.task.memory-mode tools

docs.title: Limitations and caveats
docs.text:
• Answer leakage on subprocess with shell harnesses. With bash (or any shell-capable harness) on the subprocess runtime, the agent's shell runs on the evaluator host, which also holds the Hugging Face cache with gold answers. Use the null harness for context and tools modes, and docker or prime for files mode or any shell harness.
  • Not the paper's exact samples. The mixing algorithm and judges are official, but samples are drawn here rather than taken from pre_mixed_testcases, so results are comparable in protocol but not item-for-item.
  • The judge model affects scores. Rubric categories are especially sensitive to the choice of judge. Keep the judge fixed across compared runs.
  • --select.shuffle materializes the whole selection, which downloads every needed evidence and filler file (up to ~1.2 GB evidence + ~560 MB filler, and a lot of RAM for large context sizes). Narrow the selection with categories, evidence-counts and context-sizes first.
  • Uneven folder sizes. Some category/evidence-count folders are small (e.g. user_facts with 4 evidence conversations). Round-robin draws from them until they run out.
  • BM25 is lexical. memory_search won't match paraphrases. That's part of the challenge, and the agent can fall back to listing and reading conversations.
  • Untested here: files mode has passed setup validation, but no full model run in that mode has been recorded yet.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Fix taskset 'convomem-arena' not found Install the package into the environment running the CLI: uv pip install -e . Auth error from the judge or the model Set PRIME_API_KEY, or point --client.* / --env.taskset.task.judge.* at another endpoint and key variable judge returned neither RIGHT nor WRONG The judge model isn't following the format; use a stronger or instruction-tuned judge Tool server times out at startup Raise --env.taskset.task.tools.timeout.startup; check that the package is installed for the server's Python Context-length errors in context mode Lower context-sizes, or switch to memory-mode tools Rollouts end with turn_limit Raise --env.taskset.task.max-turns, or inspect the trace for search loops Slow first run First-time Hub downloads; later runs use the HF cache (HF_HOME)
